images.title: Must fit both sides
images.purpose: Show that a tile side must divide both room lengths exactly, using a 3 ft tile that fits 12 ft but not 16 ft.
images.composition: Two horizontal strips stacked in the centre with white space above and below: the top strip fits exactly, the bottom strip leaves a gap.
exact_structure: Top strip: a bar 12 units long made of exactly 4 teal (#0072B2) squares of side 3 units, edge to edge, no gap; a grey (#6B7280) dimension line under it labelled 12 ft; a green (#009E73) tick at its right end with the word fits.

Bottom strip: a bar 16 units long made of exactly 5 teal (#0072B2) squares of side 3 units, edge to edge, followed by one vermilion (#D55E00) rectangle 1 unit wide and 3 units tall, labelled 1 ft gap; a grey (#6B7280) dimension line under the whole bar labelled 16 ft; a vermilion (#D55E00) cross at its right end with the words does not fit.
Both strips use the same square size and start at the same left edge, so the 16 ft bar is longer.
Above the top strip, one small teal (#0072B2) square with the caption 3 ft tile.
rejection: any number of squares other than 4 in the top strip and 5 in the bottom strip
the gap missing, or drawn wider than one third of a square
squares of different sizes in the two strips
images.takeaway: A tile fits only if its side divides both 12 and 16 exactly.
images.description: A 3 ft tile fits 4 times along 12 ft but leaves a 1 ft gap after 5 tiles along 16 ft.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video for this concept.
images.teaching_notes: Point out that fitting one side is not enough; the same tile must fit both sides.

image_decisions.why: The rule that a tile side must divide both lengths is clearest when students see a tile fail on one side.
